name: sort
summary: Sort lines alphabetically, numerically, by human-readable size, or by a chosen column.
compat: Ordering depends on your locale; prefix LC_ALL=C for plain byte order. -h is supported by GNU and recent BusyBox.

examples.title: Sort lines and drop duplicates
examples.explain: Prints the sorted result; the file itself is not changed.
options: Output only the first of equal lines

examples.title: Sort a CSV by its third column, numerically, largest first
examples.explain: -t, sets the field separator to a comma; -k3,3 sorts only by field 3; n compares as numbers (so 10 > 9), r reverses. The header line is sorted too; skip it with tail -n +2 data.csv | sort ...

examples.title: Biggest directories first
examples.explain: -h understands sizes like 4.0K, 12M and 1.1G. -- protects against file names that start with a dash.

name: uniq
summary: Collapse or count repeated adjacent lines (usually after sort).
compat: uniq only compares neighbouring lines, so unsorted input gives surprising results. Always sort first.

examples.title: Count how often each line occurs
examples.explain: A classic pipeline: sort groups identical lines, uniq -c counts each group, sort -rn puts the most frequent first. Great for summarising log messages.

examples.title: Show only lines that appear more than once
examples.explain: Prints one copy of each duplicated line.

name: cut
summary: Extract columns (fields) or character ranges from each line.
compat: cut handles a single-character delimiter only and does not understand quoted CSV fields. For whitespace-separated columns use awk.

examples.title: Take fields 1 and 3 from a CSV
examples.explain: -d sets the delimiter, -f picks fields (ranges like 2-4 work too).

examples.title: Usernames from /etc/passwd
examples.explain: /etc/passwd is colon-separated and readable by everyone; field 1 is the user name. It contains no passwords on modern systems.

name: tr
summary: Translate or delete characters, e.g. change case or strip Windows carriage returns.
compat: tr only reads standard input; it never takes a file name. Use < file or a pipe.

examples.title: Convert to upper case
examples.explain: Each character of the first set is replaced by the matching one in the second set.

examples.title: Strip Windows line endings into a new file
examples.explain: Fixes scripts edited on Windows that fail with '/bin/bash^M: bad interpreter' or '$'\r': command not found'. Writes to a NEW file; check it, then replace the original.
examples.warning: Never use the same file for input and output: the shell empties the output file before tr reads it, losing the contents.

examples.title: Squeeze repeated spaces
examples.explain: Replaces runs of spaces with a single space, which makes column-aligned output easier to cut.

name: sed
summary: Stream editor: print line ranges, search-and-replace, or delete lines, optionally editing files in place.
compat: -i is not POSIX. GNU and BusyBox accept -i or -i.bak; macOS/BSD sed requires an argument (-i ''). Without -i, sed only prints and never changes the file.

examples.title: Print a range of lines
examples.explain: -n turns off automatic printing, and 3,5p prints lines 3 to 5. Useful for looking at the code around a compiler error.
options: Do not print every line automatically

examples.title: Preview a replacement
examples.explain: s/old/new/g replaces every match on each line (without g only the first per line). The result goes to the terminal; the file is unchanged. Use this before -i.
options: Substitute; g = all matches in the line

examples.title: Edit a file in place, keeping a backup
examples.explain: Changes the file and saves the original as <file>.bak. Compare with diff -u <file>.bak <file>.
examples.warning: The file is rewritten. Run the same expression without -i first and check the output; keep the .bak until you have verified the result.
options: Edit in place and save a backup with the .bak suffix

examples.title: Delete comment lines from the output
examples.explain: /pattern/d deletes lines matching the regular expression; here lines starting with #.

name: awk
summary: Pattern-scanning language for columns: print fields, filter rows, sum values.
compat: The examples here use only POSIX awk features, so they work with gawk, mawk and BusyBox awk.

examples.title: Print the first column of whitespace-separated output
examples.explain: awk splits each line on runs of spaces/tabs; $1 is the first field, $NF the last. Single quotes stop the shell from treating $1 as a shell variable.
options: First field ($0 is the whole line)

examples.title: Filter CSV rows by a column value
examples.explain: -F, splits on commas. The pattern before { } chooses which lines the action runs on.

examples.title: Sum a column
examples.explain: NR is the line number; NR > 1 skips the header. END runs after the last line.

name: tee
summary: Copy a pipe's data to a file while still showing it on screen; also the right way to write a root-owned file.

examples.title: Save build output while watching it
examples.explain: 2>&1 merges error messages into the normal output so both reach the pipe. Note: the pipeline's exit status is tee's, not make's; in Bash use set -o pipefail or check ${PIPESTATUS[0]}.
examples.warning: tee without -a overwrites build.log each time.
options: Redirect stderr to wherever stdout goes

examples.title: Append instead of overwrite
examples.explain: -a adds to the end of the file, like >>.

examples.title: Append a line to a root-owned file
examples.explain: sudo echo text >> file does NOT work: the >> redirection is done by your own unprivileged shell before sudo runs. Here only tee runs as root and opens the file.
examples.warning: Writes to a system file as root. Back up the file first (sudo cp <file> <file>.bak) and double-check the file name; tee without -a would replace the whole file.
